etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English masculyne, masculyn, from Old French masculin, from Latin masculīnus, diminutive of masculus (“male, manly”), itself a diminutive of mās (“male”). Displaced native Old English werlīċ (literally “manly”).

definitions.definition: Of or pertaining to the male gender; manly.
Of or pertaining to the male sex; biologically male, not female.
Belonging to males; typically used by males.
Having the qualities stereotypically associated with men: virile, aggressive, not effeminate.

quote.citation: 1818, Henry Hallam, View of the state of Europe during the Middle ages:
quote.text: That lady, after her husband's death, held the reins with a masculine energy.

quote.citation: 1655, Thomas Fuller, The Church-history of Britain; […], London:  […]  Iohn Williams […], →OCLC, (please specify |book=I to XI):

definitions.definition: (of a noun) Being of the masculine class or grammatical gender, and inflected in that manner.
(of another part of speech) Being inflected in agreement with a masculine noun.
(grammar) Of, pertaining or belonging to the male grammatical gender, in languages that have gender distinctions.
(grammar, Mongolic languages, of any word) Having the vowel harmony of a back vowel.
(prosody) Following or ending on a stressed syllable.

quote.citation: 2009, Carlos Quiles, Fernando López-Menchero, A Grammar of Modern Indo-European, Second Edition:
quote.text: The masculine functions as the negative term in the opposition, i.e. when the gender is not defined, the masculine is used.

definitions.definition: (grammar) A word of the masculine gender.

quote.citation: 1905, George Theodore Dippold, A German grammar for high schools and colleges:
quote.text: As to the class to which the masculines of the strong declension belong, we repeat that  […]

These forces would also seem to reflect the gender distinction that can be made with respect to the divine, the feminine associated with the divine as immanent within the finite and the masculine with the divine transcendence and the infinite.

quote.citation: 1868, The Ladies' Repository, A Universalist Monthly Magazine For The Home Circle. Volume XXXIX [39]‎[1], page 458 (left column):
quote.text: I think women, at least those who do their own work, would live very simply in that respect, if there were none of the masculines to feed.
